title: Kathmandu to Syabrubesi by Jeep and Bus
meta_description: Kathmandu to Syabrubesi: 122 km, 6–8 hours. Bus, shared jeep and private jeep compared with fares, departure points, the road via Dhunche and monsoon tips.
summary: Syabrubesi is about 122 km from Kathmandu via Trishuli Bazaar and Dhunche. Local buses take 7–8 hours for about NPR 800–1,200, shared jeeps about 7 hours for NPR 1,500–2,500, and a private jeep 6–7 hours for about NPR 15,000–20,000 per vehicle. Start early and allow extra time in the monsoon.

sections.heading: The route and how long it takes
paras: The road to Syabrubesi leaves Kathmandu through the northern suburbs and climbs over the rim of the valley at Kakani, where on clear mornings you see the Ganesh Himal and Langtang peaks ahead. It then drops to Trishuli Bazaar (also called Bidur) on the Trishuli River and follows the river north to Betrawati. From there the Pasang Lhamu Highway climbs steep switchbacks to Dhunche (1,960 m), the district headquarters and national park gate, before descending to Syabrubesi on the Bhote Koshi.

The distance is about 122 km, but this is a mountain road, so plan on 6–7 hours by private jeep and 7–8 hours by bus. The first 70 km to Betrawati is mostly paved and busy; the last 50 km is narrower, with rough sections, hairpin bends and landslide-prone slopes. Delays happen from road works, traffic leaving Kathmandu and, in the monsoon, landslides that can close the road for hours.

sections.heading: Taking the local bus
paras: Public buses to Syabrubesi leave from the Machhapokhari and Gongabu (New Bus Park) area on Kathmandu's Ring Road, mainly between about 6:30 and 8 am. Tickets are sold at counters the day before or on the morning; buying a day ahead secures a seat near the front, which helps with travel sickness. Luggage goes on the roof under a tarpaulin, so pack valuables in a daypack you keep with you.

The bus stops frequently to pick up passengers, goods and sometimes livestock, and there is a lunch break at a roadside restaurant, usually around Trishuli or Kalikasthan. Seats are narrow and legroom tight for taller travellers. It is the cheapest way and a real slice of Nepali life, but after seven or eight hours on winding roads most trekkers arrive tired.

Keep passport and permits in your daypack for the Dhunche checkpoint

sections.heading: Shared and private jeeps
paras: Shared jeeps leave from the same area of north Kathmandu and set off once all seats are sold. They are quicker than buses and stop less, but seating is tight, typically three in the back row, and departure times depend on demand. They suit solo trekkers or couples who want to save time without paying for a whole vehicle.

A private jeep or 4WD is the most comfortable and flexible choice and what most agencies, including us, use for packages. The driver collects you at your hotel, usually around 7 am, and you stop when you want for photographs, tea or toilets. For a group of four to six, the per-person cost is close to a shared jeep seat. Private jeeps also make sense for families with children, older travellers and anyone prone to travel sickness.

sections.heading: The Dhunche checkpoint and permits
paras: Just before Dhunche, vehicles stop at the Langtang National Park gate. Trekkers show the park entry permit and passport, and staff may check TIMS cards and guide details. If you have not yet bought the park permit, it can be purchased here, but it is simpler to arrange it in Kathmandu through your agency. The check usually takes 10–20 minutes, longer when several buses arrive at once.

Gosaikunda trekkers get off at Dhunche, the trailhead, while Langtang Valley and Tamang Heritage Trail trekkers continue about 15 km and one hour further to Syabrubesi. The road beyond Syabrubesi continues to Rasuwagadhi, the border crossing to Tibet used by Kailash overland yatras via Kerung.

sections.heading: What to see on the drive
paras: The drive is long, but it is not wasted time. Climbing out of Kathmandu, the road crosses the valley rim at Kakani, at about 2,000 m, where clear mornings bring a view of the Ganesh Himal, Langtang Lirung and the peaks along the Tibetan border. A short stop here is worth it if the sky is clear. The road then drops through pine forest and terraced hills to Trishuli Bazaar, a busy market town on the Trishuli River, where many buses pause.

North of Betrawati, the valley narrows and the road climbs steeply past Kalikasthan, with views down to the river and across to Tamang villages clinging to the slopes. Look out for the Trishuli and Upper Trishuli hydropower works along the way. From the switchbacks below Dhunche, the Ganesh Himal appears again to the west. The final descent to Syabrubesi follows the Bhote Koshi, which flows down from Tibet, past landslide scars that show how often this road is rebuilt.

sections.heading: Monsoon, safety and travel sickness
paras: From June to September, heavy rain causes landslides on the road above Betrawati, and the road can be blocked for hours or occasionally days. If you travel in this season, check conditions the evening before, carry snacks and water, and keep a spare day in your schedule. Drivers sometimes wait for bulldozers to clear debris or arrange for passengers to walk past a blockage to a vehicle on the other side.

Even in the dry season, the winding road upsets many stomachs. Eat a light breakfast, sit near the front, look at the horizon, and take travel-sickness tablets 30 minutes before departure if you are prone to it. Travelling by daylight in a private jeep with an experienced driver is the safest option, and we avoid night driving on this road entirely.

sections.heading: Getting back to Kathmandu
paras: Return buses and jeeps leave Syabrubesi early, mostly between 7 and 8 am, arriving in Kathmandu in the afternoon. Lodge owners can book bus tickets the evening before. Private jeeps can be arranged through your agency. Avoid booking an international flight on the same day as the return drive, as road delays are common. A night in Kathmandu, or at a quieter hotel on the city's northern edge near Shivapuri, gives a buffer before flying home.

faqs.q: How far is Syabrubesi from Kathmandu?
faqs.a: About 122 km by road via Kakani, Trishuli Bazaar, Betrawati and Dhunche. Despite the modest distance, the mountain road takes 6–7 hours by private jeep and 7–8 hours by bus, and longer during monsoon landslides. Start early to arrive in daylight.

faqs.q: What time does the bus to Syabrubesi leave?
faqs.a: Buses to Syabrubesi generally leave the Machhapokhari and Gongabu area of Kathmandu between about 6:30 and 8 am. There may be one or two later departures, but early buses are best to arrive before dark. Times change, so check current status the day before.

faqs.q: How much is a jeep from Kathmandu to Syabrubesi?
faqs.a: A private jeep costs roughly NPR 15,000–20,000 one way for the vehicle, seating up to five or six passengers with luggage. Shared jeep seats cost about NPR 1,500–2,500 per person. Prices rise during festivals and with fuel prices; check current rates before you travel.

faqs.q: Is the Kathmandu to Syabrubesi road dangerous?
faqs.a: It is a narrow mountain road with steep drops and landslide-prone sections, especially above Betrawati and in the monsoon. Thousands of vehicles use it safely each year. Travel in daylight, choose an experienced driver or private jeep, and check conditions before travelling in heavy rain.

faqs.q: Can I get off at Dhunche for Gosaikunda?
faqs.a: Yes. All buses and jeeps to Syabrubesi pass through Dhunche, the trailhead for Gosaikunda, about an hour before Syabrubesi. Tell the conductor or driver in advance. Dhunche has lodges for the night before you start walking.

faqs.q: Is there a tourist bus to Syabrubesi?
faqs.a: Occasionally some operators run more comfortable tourist-style buses in peak season, but most departures are local buses. Shared and private jeeps fill the gap for travellers wanting more comfort. Ask your agency or hotel for current options a day or two before travel.

faqs.q: Where do I buy bus tickets to Syabrubesi?
faqs.a: Bus tickets are sold at counters in the Machhapokhari and Gongabu bus park area in north Kathmandu, ideally the day before travel. Your hotel or trekking agency can buy them for a small fee. On the return, lodges in Syabrubesi can book seats the evening before.

No, there is no airport at Syabrubesi or Dhunche. The only air option is a charter helicopter, which takes about 30 minutes but is expensive and mainly used for emergencies or for flying out from Kyanjin Gompa at the end of a trek.

faqs.q: How do I avoid travel sickness on the road to Syabrubesi?
faqs.a: Eat a light breakfast, sit near the front, keep a window slightly open, look at the horizon rather than your phone, and take travel-sickness tablets 30 minutes before departure. A private jeep allows more stops and a smoother ride than a crowded bus.
